title: Variables, Types & Zero Values
summary: Go is statically typed: every variable has a type fixed at compile time. You declare variables with `var` or the short form `:=`, and crucially, a variable with no explicit value is never garbage — it gets its type's **zero value** (0, "", false, or nil). This guarantee eliminates a whole class of uninitialized-memory bugs.

subtopics.title: Declaring with var
subtopics.explanation: `var name type` declares a variable; you can add an initializer. With an initializer the type can be omitted and is inferred. `var` works at package and function scope.
subtopics.example:
var count int        // zero value 0
var name = "Ada"     // type inferred: string

subtopics.title: Short declaration :=
subtopics.explanation: Inside functions, `name := value` declares and initializes in one step, inferring the type. It can't be used at package scope and can't omit the value. It's the most common form you'll write.

subtopics.title: Zero values
subtopics.explanation: A declared-but-uninitialized variable holds its type's zero value: 0 for numbers, false for bool, "" for string, and nil for pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, and interfaces. There is no 'undefined'.
subtopics.example:
var n int     // 0
var s string  // ""
var p *int    // nil

subtopics.title: Basic types
subtopics.explanation: Go has sized integers (int, int8..int64, uint...), floats (float32, float64), bool, string, and the alias byte (uint8) and rune (int32 for Unicode code points). `int` is 64-bit on modern platforms.
subtopics.example:
var b byte = 65   // 'A'
var r rune = '世'  // a Unicode code point

subtopics.title: Explicit type conversion
subtopics.explanation: Go has no implicit numeric conversions — mixing types is a compile error. You must convert explicitly with T(x). This prevents silent precision loss and surprising coercions.
subtopics.example:
var i int = 3
var f float64 = float64(i) // explicit, required

subtopics.title: Constants vs variables
subtopics.explanation: Variables can change; constants (next topic) are fixed at compile time. Untyped constants like 42 adapt to the context, which is why x := 42 becomes int but var f float64 = 42 becomes a float.

foundations.overview: In Go, every variable has a single, fixed type known when the program compiles — you can't put a string into an int variable later. You declare variables either with the explicit `var` keyword or the concise `:=` short form inside functions. The defining Go feature here is zero values: if you declare a variable without giving it a value, Go doesn't leave it pointing at random memory — it initializes it to a well-defined zero (0, false, "", or nil depending on the type). This makes Go code predictable and removes the uninitialized-variable bugs common in C.
foundations.formalDefinition: A variable is a typed, named storage location. Go is statically and strongly typed: types are checked at compile time and not implicitly converted. Any variable declared without an explicit initializer is set to the zero value of its type.
foundations.whyItMatters: Variables and types are the bedrock of every program. Go's zero-value guarantee and lack of implicit conversions shape how you write safe, idiomatic code, and questions about zero values and type conversions are extremely common in interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each variable as a labeled, pre-formatted box sized for exactly one type. If you don't put anything in it, it isn't empty in a dangerous way — it comes with a sensible default already inside (0, "", false, or nil).
foundations.runtimePerspective: The compiler allocates storage sized to the type and zeroes it. Because zeroing is built into allocation, constructing a struct or slice gives you safe defaults for free; the runtime never hands you uninitialized memory.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Designing structs whose zero value is already usable (e.g. sync.Mutex, bytes.Buffer), accumulating counters that start at 0, and using nil as 'absent' for pointers and maps.
foundations.businessImpact: Predictable defaults and compile-time type checking catch bugs before deployment, reducing production incidents and the cost of fixing them later.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Designing types whose zero value is meaningful ('make the zero value useful') leads to simpler APIs that need no explicit initialization.
foundations.performanceImpact: Zeroing memory on allocation is cheap and lets the runtime skip separate initialization passes; fixed types let the compiler choose efficient machine representations.
commonUseCases: Counters and accumulators starting at zero
Structs designed to be usable at their zero value
Using nil as the 'not present' value for pointers/maps

commonMisconceptions.myth: An unassigned variable is undefined or random.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's the type's zero value — 0, false, "", or nil — always well-defined.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go converts between number types automatically.
commonMisconceptions.reality: There are no implicit conversions; you must write float64(i) or int(f) explicitly.
Short declaration only works inside functions and requires an initializer; package-level declarations use var.

visualExplorer.caption: What the compiler does when you declare a variable.

config.intro: From declaration to a usable, zeroed variable:

steps.name: Determine the type
steps.detail: Either you state it (var x int) or the compiler infers it from the initializer (x := 42 -> int).

steps.name: Allocate storage
steps.detail: The compiler reserves memory sized for that exact type.

steps.name: Apply the zero value
steps.detail: If there's no initializer, the storage is set to the type's zero: 0, false, "", or nil.

steps.name: Or store the initializer
steps.detail: If you gave a value, it's stored, after any explicit conversion you wrote (Go never converts implicitly).

steps.name: Use it safely
steps.detail: Because there's no uninitialized state, reading the variable always yields a defined value.

interactiveExamples.title: Zero values of the basic types
interactiveExamples.explanation: Each variable is declared with var and no initializer, so each holds its type's zero value. The %q verb quotes the string so the empty string is visible.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: fix the type mismatch
interactiveExamples.explanation: Go won't add an int and a float64 directly — that's a compile error. Convert one explicitly so the types match, then print the sum.

code.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	i := 3                       // int
	f := 2.5                     // float64
	sum := float64(i) + f        // explicit conversion required
	fmt.Println(sum)             // 5.5
}

checkpoints.code:
var s string
var n int
fmt.Printf("%q %d\n", s, n)
checkpoints.explanation: The zero value of a string is the empty string (printed as "" by %q) and the zero value of an int is 0. Strings are never nil — that's only for pointers, slices, maps, etc.

options: Mismatched types: int * float64 needs an explicit conversion
checkpoints.explanation: Go has no implicit numeric conversion. int and float64 can't be multiplied directly; write float64(x) * y. This strictness prevents silent precision bugs.

checkpoints.prompt: Which declaration is INVALID at package scope (outside any function)?
checkpoints.explanation: The short form := only works inside functions. At package scope you must use var (with or without an explicit type/initializer).

checkpoints.code:
var b byte = 65
var r rune = 'A'
fmt.Println(b, r)
checkpoints.explanation: byte (uint8) and rune (int32) are integer types, so Println shows their numeric values. 'A' is the code point 65. To print the character, convert to string: string(r).

codeLab.title: Summarize with a zero-value-friendly type
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Average(nums []int) float64` returning the mean of nums, or 0 when nums is empty. Lean on int's zero value (0) for the running sum and handle the empty case cleanly.
hints: Accumulate into an int sum starting at its zero value.
Convert both sum and len to float64 explicitly before dividing.

debuggingLab.title: The average is wrong (integer division)
debuggingLab.symptom: Average of 1 and 2 prints 1 instead of 1.5.

brokenCode.code:
a, b := 1, 2
avg := (a + b) / 2     // both ints -> integer division
fmt.Println(float64(avg)) // converts AFTER truncation

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Because a and b are ints, (a+b)/2 is integer division: 3/2 = 1, dropping the fraction. Converting to float64 afterward is too late — the precision is already gone. You must convert before dividing.
commonMistakes: Dividing ints then converting, instead of converting then dividing.
Assuming Go promotes ints to floats automatically in division.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Convert to float64 before the division so the fractional part survives.

solution.code:
a, b := 1, 2
avg := float64(a+b) / 2.0  // convert first, then divide
fmt.Println(avg)           // 1.5

theory.question: What are zero values in Go and why do they matter?
theory.directAnswer: A zero value is the default a variable gets when declared without an explicit initializer: 0 for numeric types, false for bool, "" for string, and nil for pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, and interfaces. They matter because they guarantee every variable starts in a well-defined state — Go has no uninitialized/undefined memory — which removes a whole class of bugs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The default value of each type, applied automatically on declaration.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make programs predictable and safe by eliminating uninitialized memory.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Allocation zeroes the storage; the type determines what 'zero' means.

theory.whyImportant: Designing types whose zero value is useful is idiomatic Go and a common interview theme.
theory.realWorldExample: A sync.Mutex and bytes.Buffer are usable immediately at their zero value — no constructor needed.

followUps.question: What's the zero value of a slice?
followUps.answer: nil — a nil slice has len 0 and cap 0 but you can still append to and range over it.

followUps.question: Is a string ever nil?
followUps.answer: No — strings are value types; their zero value is the empty string "".

theory.question: Why does Go require explicit type conversions, and when do you need them?
theory.directAnswer: Go is strongly typed and performs no implicit numeric conversions, so mixing types (like int and float64) in an expression is a compile error. You convert explicitly with T(x) — e.g. float64(i) or int(f) — whenever types differ. This prevents silent precision loss and surprising coercions.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Mandatory, explicit conversions between distinct types.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make data-type changes visible and intentional, avoiding hidden bugs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The conversion T(x) produces a new value of type T from x; the compiler enforces it where types differ.

theory.whyImportant: Integer-division and type-mismatch bugs are common; explicit conversion is the fix.
theory.realWorldExample: Computing a ratio: float64(hits) / float64(total) to avoid integer division.

followUps.question: Does := perform conversion?
followUps.answer: No — := only infers the type of the initializer; it never converts between types.

scenario.question: You design a Config struct. How can zero values make its API simpler, and what's the risk?
scenario.directAnswer: Design fields so the zero value is a sensible default — then callers can use Config{} directly and only set what they need. The risk is ambiguity: for some fields 0 or "" is a legitimate value AND the 'unset' signal, so you can't tell them apart. Use a pointer (*int) or a bool 'set' flag when you must distinguish 'unset' from a real zero.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Leveraging zero values for default-friendly struct APIs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go idiom 'make the zero value useful' reduces boilerplate constructors.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Unset struct fields are already zeroed; only override what differs.

scenario.whyImportant: Good zero-value design is a hallmark of idiomatic Go APIs.
scenario.realWorldExample: http.Server{} works with sensible defaults; you set only Addr and Handler.

followUps.question: How do you tell 'unset' from a real 0?
followUps.answer: Use a pointer field (*int): nil means unset, &0 means an explicit zero.

coding.question: Implement func CelsiusToF(c float64) float64 and explain why type conversions matter here.
coding.thoughtProcess: The formula is c*9/5 + 32. Keep everything float64 to preserve fractions; if c were an int we'd need an explicit conversion to avoid integer division.
coding.lineByLine: c is float64, and the literals 9.0/5.0/32.0 are floats too, so the arithmetic stays floating-point and 37.0 maps to 98.6 rather than being truncated. If c were an int, c*9/5 would do integer division — we'd convert with float64(c) first.

followUps.question: What if the input were an int temperature?
followUps.answer: Convert first: float64(c)*9/5 + 32, otherwise integer division loses precision.

followUps.question: What's the zero-value behavior?
followUps.answer: CelsiusToF(0) returns 32 — a perfectly valid result, no special-casing needed.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Idiomatic Go favors types whose zero value is immediately useful, reducing the need for constructors and initialization order dependencies across packages.
productionDeepDive.performance: Compile-time fixed types let the compiler pick efficient machine representations; zeroing on allocation is cheap and avoids separate init passes.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Some standard types (sync.Mutex, sync.WaitGroup) are designed to be used at their zero value, which simplifies concurrent code — never copy them after first use, though.
productionDeepDive.reliability: The zero-value guarantee plus no implicit conversions catch many bugs at compile time; combine with go vet to flag suspicious conversions and shadowing.
productionDeepDive.observability: Be explicit when 0/""/false could be a real value vs. 'unset' in metrics and configs; use pointers or sentinels to avoid misreporting.
productionDeepDive.security: Strong typing prevents accidental data coercion; avoid converting between signed/unsigned without range checks to prevent overflow surprises in size/length math.

caseStudies.solution: Design types like bytes.Buffer and sync.Mutex to be usable at the zero value.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Must document that zero value is valid and that some types can't be copied.
caseStudies.lessons: A useful zero value makes APIs simpler and safer.

caseStudies.problem: Distinguishing 'unset' from a real zero in request bodies.
caseStudies.solution: Use pointer fields so nil means absent.
caseStudies.lessons: Pointers disambiguate unset from a legitimate zero value.

keyTakeaways: Go is statically typed: every variable's type is fixed at compile time.
Declare with var (any scope) or := (inside functions, requires an initializer); := infers the type.
Uninitialized variables get a well-defined zero value: 0, false, "", or nil — never undefined memory.
There are no implicit conversions; convert explicitly with T(x), e.g. float64(i), to avoid bugs like integer division.
